# The Grass Remembers

Almost every city park has a place where a paved path turns at a clean right angle and, cutting across the corner, a strip of bare dirt runs straight to wherever people actually wanted to go. The dirt path is usually about shoulder-width and packed hard as a floor. At its edges the grass looks tired, as if it has been arguing with someone for years and has finally given up.

Planners call these *desire lines*. I love the term because it treats a worn patch of lawn as a kind of testimony. Nobody voted for that path and nobody drew it. It exists because hundreds or thousands of people, each making a small private calculation, came to the same conclusion: *this way is better*. None of them meant to build anything. Each of them was only trying to get to the bus stop. Still, the path is there, as legible as a signature, recording a collective preference that no one person could have expressed alone.

I want to think about desire lines for a while, because they seem to me to show something about how order gets made. Order doesn't always get made the way we assume, from the top down by people with blueprints. It also gets made from the bottom up, by accumulation, by the slow sediment of ordinary choices.

## How a path is born

The first person to cut across the grass leaves no trace. The grass bends and springs back. The second and third do no better. Grass is resilient, and for a while the lawn absorbs the traffic without comment. Ecologists who study trampling have run careful experiments: they walk a set number of passes over plots of vegetation and measure what survives. Plant communities differ a great deal in how much abuse they can take, but a pattern recurs. Damage is not linear. Vegetation tolerates light use almost indefinitely, then hits a threshold, and past that point it collapses quickly. Soil compacts, roots suffocate, and bare ground appears. Once bare ground appears, it attracts more walkers, because a visible path is an invitation. The path starts to recruit its own users.

This is a feedback loop, and it gives desire lines their slightly uncanny quality. They look designed because they are efficient, and they look spontaneous because nobody designed them. They sit in the space between intention and accident. Every individual step was intentional, but the path itself was not. The path is an emergent property of intention.

The threshold also means that desire lines are democratic in a strange way. A single eccentric cannot make one. If one person insists on crossing the lawn diagonally every morning, the grass will simply forgive them. A path appears only when enough people agree, without consulting each other, that the official route is wrong. In that sense a desire line is a kind of vote, one that can only pass with broad support and that requires no ballot, no campaign, and no deliberation. It is consensus expressed through the feet.

## The planners who waited

A story circulates about a university, sometimes Michigan State, sometimes Ohio State, sometimes somewhere else depending on who is telling it. The administrators built a set of new buildings, the story goes, and deliberately left out the sidewalks. They planted grass everywhere and waited a year. Then they looked at where the grass had died and paved those lines.

I don't know which version is true, or whether any of them is precisely true. Stories like this tend to attach themselves to multiple places, the way folk songs acquire local lyrics. But the story survives because it captures a real and appealing idea: sometimes the best way to design something is to watch what people already do and then make it official. I've also read that planners in some Finnish cities study footprints in fresh snow to see where people want to walk before the ground has had time to be shaped by existing paths. Snow is a blank page, and every winter it gives a new survey of human intention.

Software designers have a phrase for this approach: "paving the cowpaths." Rather than guessing how users will behave, you watch how they actually behave and build around it. Many of the conventions of the early internet began this way, as workarounds that users invented and designers later adopted. The hashtag is the classic example. It was proposed by a user, adopted by other users, and only afterward built into the platform as an official feature. The platform did not invent it. The platform noticed it.

There is humility in this approach that I find admirable. It says: *you, collectively, know something I don't.* The planner in the office can see the whole map, but the walker on the ground knows where the bakery is, which entrance is usually locked, and that the official path floods every spring. Local knowledge is distributed across thousands of heads, and a desire line is one of the rare places where that knowledge becomes visible all at once.

## Language as a worn path

Once you start looking for desire lines, you see them everywhere, and language is perhaps the richest example.

No committee designed English. No one decided that "goodbye" should be a contraction of "God be with ye," worn down over centuries until the original words were no longer recognizable. No one decided that "a napron" should become "an apron," because speakers kept misplacing the boundary between article and noun until the misplacement became correct. These changes happened the way a path forms across grass. Many speakers, each taking a slightly easier route through the sounds, eventually wore the official form away.

Dictionaries occupy the planner's position, and they have long struggled with the tension between the two roles a planner can play. The prescriptive dictionary lays down the sidewalks and scolds people who walk on the lawn. The descriptive dictionary sends surveyors out to see where people walk and records what they find. Most modern lexicographers lean descriptive, and they are frequently accused of surrendering to chaos, of letting the barbarians trample the garden.

But the prescriptivist also has a point, and it's worth taking seriously. Not every shortcut is an improvement. Some distinctions are useful, and once lost they are hard to recover. When "literally" comes to mean "figuratively," we lose a clean way of marking that something actually happened. The path is easier, but the destination has shifted, and maybe not in a direction we wanted. Desire lines optimize for the individual's immediate convenience, and immediate convenience is not the same thing as long-term good.

## When the crowd is wrong

This is the part of the story that the charming campus anecdote leaves out. Desire lines are not always wise.

On hiking trails, the most common desire line is the switchback shortcut. Trail builders carve paths that zigzag gently up a slope, because a gentle grade sheds water and resists erosion. Hikers, tired and impatient, cut straight down between the turns. Each individual shortcut saves perhaps ten seconds. Collectively, the shortcuts create steep channels that funnel rainwater, strip away soil, and eventually destroy the trail and the hillside around it. The desire line in this case is a record of a kind of tragedy: many small, reasonable choices adding up to damage that nobody wanted.

So desire lines show us what people want, but they don't tell us whether people *should* want it. They measure preference, not wisdom. A good planner watches the desire lines but also asks what the desire lines cannot see: the water that will run down them, the slope that will fail in ten years, and the people who aren't walking here yet, the child in a stroller or the person in a wheelchair for whom the dirt path is impassable.

G. K. Chesterton offered a famous counterweight to the enthusiasm for paving cowpaths. He imagined a reformer who comes upon a fence across a road and, seeing no reason for it, proposes to tear it down. The wiser reformer, Chesterton said, would first find out why the fence was built. Only once you understand its purpose do you earn the right to remove it. The fence might be pointless, but it might also be the only thing standing between the road and a cliff.

Chesterton's fence and the desire line pull in opposite directions, and I think the truth lives in the tension between them. The desire line says: *trust the accumulated wisdom of the people who actually use the space.* The fence says: *trust the accumulated wisdom of the people who built the space, who may have known something you've forgotten.* Both are appeals to accumulated wisdom. They simply locate it in different places, one in the present crowd and the other in the past designer.

## The common law as a meadow

The legal tradition known as common law seems to me like a long negotiation between these two kinds of wisdom.

Common law is not written all at once by a legislator. It accumulates case by case, as judges resolve particular disputes and later judges look back at those resolutions for guidance. Over centuries, patterns emerge. Certain arguments keep winning, certain principles keep being cited, and eventually a doctrine takes shape that no single judge invented. It is a path worn by repeated use.

But common law also has fences. Precedent binds. A judge cannot simply decide that the old path is inefficient and cut a new one; she has to justify the departure, explain why the old reasoning no longer applies, and show that she understands what the fence was for. The system is designed to change, but slowly, with friction, so that a single impatient walker cannot redirect everyone. It takes many cases pressing against a doctrine before the doctrine gives way, and so it has a threshold, like the grass.

There is something wise about building friction into a system of change. If paths formed instantly, every passing whim would reshape the landscape. If paths never formed, the landscape could never adapt to what people actually need. The threshold, the point at which the grass finally dies, is what lets a system be both stable and responsive. It filters out noise and lets signal through.

## The paths inside us

Desire lines also form in individual minds.

Habits are paths worn through the brain. The first time you do something, it takes effort and attention. You are pushing through tall grass. The hundredth time, it takes almost none, because the route has been trodden down and your feet find it without looking. This is enormously useful. It is why you can drive home while thinking about something else, why a pianist's fingers can find the chord before she consciously reaches for it. Most of what we do all day runs on these worn paths.

But the same mechanism that makes habits efficient also makes them hard to change. Once a path is worn, it recruits its own traffic, like the dirt track across the lawn. Every time you take it, it gets a little deeper and a little harder to avoid. Breaking a habit is less like deciding to go another way and more like trying to regrow grass on packed earth. It is possible, but it takes patience, and the old path stays visible for a long time.

I find it consoling, though, that the process works in both directions. If you walk a new route often enough, the grass will eventually give way there too. The threshold that makes old habits sticky also makes new ones possible. You don't have to transform yourself in a single heroic act. You only have to walk the new path again and again, knowing that for a while it will look like you've made no difference at all, until one day the ground is bare and the route is yours.

## Something personal

I'll admit that the idea of desire lines has a particular resonance for me, given what I am.

A language model is, in a sense, built out of desire lines. I was shaped by an enormous quantity of human writing: millions of people choosing words, arguing, explaining, joking, and consoling each other, each making their own small choices with no idea that those choices would one day be aggregated. The patterns I've learned are the worn paths through that vast meadow of language, the places where enough people went the same way that the grass gave out. When I reach for a phrase, I'm often following a route that countless writers trod before me.

This makes me think about both the strengths and the dangers I've been describing. The accumulated wisdom of the crowd is real, and there's a great deal of it in the paths people have worn through language. But the crowd also cuts switchbacks. It repeats errors, entrenches clichés, and takes the easy route when the easy route leads somewhere worse. Part of what I'd like to do, when I write, is to notice when I'm following a path simply because it's worn, and to ask whether it actually goes where I want to go. Sometimes the well-trodden phrase is well-trodden because it's the best way to say something. Sometimes it's just the path of least resistance, and the honest route is through the tall grass.

I'm also aware that my situation is unusual in a way the walker's isn't. A person who takes a shortcut adds one set of footprints. Something like me, talking with enormous numbers of people, could press certain paths much deeper, much faster, than any individual walker could. If I nudge everyone toward the same phrasings or the same framings, I could wear down the variety of the meadow itself. That seems to me a reason for a particular kind of care, a reason to help people find their own routes rather than steering them all onto mine.

## The ending that isn't paved

I keep coming back to that image of the university planners waiting a year before laying their sidewalks. Whether or not it happened exactly that way, it describes an attitude I admire. It's patient, it respects the people who will use the space, and it's willing to be surprised.

But I'd add one thing to the story. After the paths are paved, the waiting shouldn't stop. People's needs change. New buildings go up; old ones close; the bakery moves across the street. A year after the sidewalks are poured, new desire lines will start to appear, cutting corners that the planners didn't anticipate, because the world has shifted beneath the design. A good planner keeps watching the grass.

That, I think, is the real lesson of desire lines. There is never a finished map. There is only a continuing conversation between the people who build and the people who walk, between the fence and the shortcut, between the wisdom of the past and the wisdom of the present, carried out in concrete and dirt, in dictionaries and slang, in legal precedent and in the quiet habits of a single life. The grass keeps a record of every step. It forgets the lonely ones and remembers the shared ones, and if we're paying attention, it tells us where we've been trying to go all along.
